prize_parts.citation: for a poetry that has renewed the Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a sustained argument with inherited forms, together with the poetics that belongs to the same project

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged after the exchange. My citation is narrower in scope. The case for Adonis rests on formal and linguistic achievement across a long, fully formed body of work: Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses are the works the list names for a poetry that reworks the idiom of Arabic verse through myth and fragmentation while arguing with the classical tradition. The voice is distinctive, and the intellectual depth comes from a poetics worked out alongside the poems. The citation now names the poetry as the object of the prize and the poetics as part of the same project. Carlberg's and Sward's round-1 formulations pushed me toward this, and I accept Sward's condition: if the poems cannot carry the case, the essays cannot carry it for them. I do not count the colleagues' agreement as merit. The three Adonis positions overlap heavily, and I treat that overlap as a reason to test the claim harder, not as support for it. Having done that, I still judge that a renewal of a poetic language is the more durable kind of distinctiveness, and that the oeuvre can be assessed as a whole now.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 stand and the exchange did not remove them. The core of the claim lies in Arabic prosody, diction and intertextual allusion, which I can reach only through translations and secondary accounts. Historical and critical influence on later Arabic poetry has to be kept apart from the quality of individual poems. Public political positions must not enter the judgement. The chair's question to the Adonis supporters, which later collections show deepening rather than repetition, has no answer in the record available to me. I can only point, with caution, to the later long poetic projects and the essayistic poetics as public knowledge, and I cannot verify their quality or how fully they are translated. Cărtărescu's case is strong on imaginative depth and control of very long structures. Its main open test, the later volumes and the moral range, is not resolved by my reading either. If the committee cannot establish confidence in the poems themselves, I would not insist on Adonis, and I could support Cărtărescu as the final recommendation.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg holds that large narrative architecture survives partial translation loss better than prosodic and intertextual effects, presents this as a point about assessability under uncertainty and not greater merit, and argues that a decades-old body of work can be assessed now on its major works.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between assessability and merit, and it is the fairest statement of the disagreement between us. I agree that durability is not decided by the length of a reception history, and that 'remains to be tested' should not become a reason to defer. I would apply the same rule to Adonis: if the established central works carry the case, the committee should not ask for more. Where I still differ is that the prosodic and allusive core is exactly what we cannot test directly, so the Adonis case needs a closer reading of the Arabic than I can supply. For Cărtărescu, sentence-level density is also a feature of the original that translation may flatten, so I do not see the narrative-architecture argument as a clean advantage. It is a real reason to rank him close behind, and I am prepared to support him if the Arabic reading cannot be secured.

responses.point: Mattson makes distinctness of voice the criterion she finds hardest to meet and places Cărtărescu first. She says that if the human dimension does not hold in the late volumes, the case narrows to virtuosity of design, and she would then weigh Adonis or Michon more heavily. She asks what in the poems themselves is distinct from the importance of the renewal.
responses.response: That question is the right one to put to me. My answer, with the same translation caveat, is that the distinctiveness lies in how the poems handle myth and fragmentation as a poetic procedure, and in the way they work against inherited forms. The historical weight of that renewal is a separate matter and should not be counted twice. I cannot demonstrate it line by line from the supplied record, and I do not claim to. I take her conditional seriously: if the late Cărtărescu volumes do not keep their human range, the choice between us narrows. If the Adonis poems cannot be shown to carry the claim apart from his influence, her own condition applies to me as well. I record that her first alternative is a candidate I could support.

responses.point: Swärd drafts a citation that treats the poetic language as the object of the prize and the criticism as one project, adds that the essays should not carry the case if the poems cannot, and says Cărtărescu would be the more defensible choice if the committee cannot reach confidence about the poetry itself.
responses.response: I adopt her condition and have written it into my citation. I also take her fallback seriously, because it states honestly what confidence in the poetry would have to mean. Her point that the lyric and corpus-coverage limits apply to both candidates is correct, and I withdraw any suggestion that the translation risk is smaller on one side. Where I would go further is on the question she and Olsson-type readings leave open, whether Adonis's later decades deepen the project. We both say the record is thin there. A final recommendation should say so openly and not present the later work as established.

responses.point: Palm places Anne Carson first for a voice joining classical scholarship, lyric, narrative and book-object form. She names the reservations herself: the work is hybrid and idiosyncratic, its reception is concentrated in Anglophone culture, and book-object forms travel poorly. She says she would move toward Cărtărescu if the later-volume question is clarified.
responses.response: I respect how openly she states the limits of her own case, and I accept that the classical engagement is a through-line of method. My remaining difficulty is the chair's question, and I have no new evidence on it: which works beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox show sustained development, and can the verbal and narrative work be separated from the object forms? Until that is answered I do not think the whole-oeuvre case is established, and I would not make translation part of a citation for her, since it is not a genre listed for the entry. Her stated openness to Cărtărescu matters. It means her alternative and the second choice of the three Adonis supporters coincide, and that is a reason to examine the Cărtărescu case closely and not an argument for him.

uncertainties: Arabic prosody, diction and allusion cannot be tested directly by me. My view of the poems rests on translations and secondary accounts, and I have not independently verified the texts or the full bibliography.

Whether the later decades of Adonis's work deepen the project or repeat it is not settled by the record available to me, and I cannot name later collections whose quality and translation coverage I have verified.
How the poetics should be weighed against the poems in a citation, and how critical influence can be separated from poetic quality, remain open. The narrowed citation is a provisional answer.

The comparison with Cărtărescu turns on weighing a language-level renewal against a large prose architecture whose late volumes and poetry I cannot assess directly. Reasonable members may weigh these differently, and I do not claim my weighting is neutral.

No ballot has four explicit supporters. The committee has publicly said it seeks outside expert reports where the Academy lacks deep competence, and a recommendation on Adonis should state its reliance on translations and such reports. I do not regard a no-award outcome as warranted by translation limits that apply to every candidate writing outside the committee's own languages, but I do not exclude it if confidence cannot be reached.
Can Xue, Carson, Zurita and Michon are assessed here only through the shortlist descriptions and public knowledge. My ranking of them is not a considered rejection.
statement.conflict_note: No documented personal, institutional or translation connection to Adonis or any other shortlisted writer appears in my profile. For transparency, my scholarly work on modern poetry, the literary fragment and exile literature is thematically close to the fragmentation and tradition-argument described in the Adonis entry. That is context and not evidence of preference, and I have not recused myself. I chair the committee and hold B004 as my own first choice, as the chair summary discloses. Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented and her vote is a modeling assumption. This simulation is a committee recommendation, and the full Academy decides. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
